								Politics								
							
							
					
					Markey is favored to win by 23 points, according to late September polling by UNH.

					
	
	Moderator Jon Keller, left, listens during Tuesday's debate between US Senate nominee John Deaton, center, and Senator Ed Markey at WBZ-TV's studio in Boston. WBZ-TV

				In three weeks, Democratic incumbent Sen. Ed Markey and Republican John Deaton will face off on ballots across the commonwealth. But first, the two Senate candidates met in an antagonistic debate Tuesday evening — the only scheduled debate between the two before the Nov. 3 election.The debate, hosted by WBZ-TV’s John Keller, pitted longtime politician Markey, 80, against a relative political newcomer in 59-year-old Deaton. The Republican nominee first entered the Massachusetts political scene in 2024, when he challenged Sen. Elizabeth Warren and lost by a nearly 20-point margin.Deaton, a lawyer who specializes in representing asbestos poisoning victims and advocates for cryptocurrency, ran unopposed in the Republican primary earlier this year. Markey defeated Rep. Seth Moulton by nearly 30 points in the Sept. 1 Democratic primary.Advertisement:According to late September polling by UNH, Markey is favored to defeat Deaton by 23 points to win what would be his third full term as senator. If Deaton were to win, he would be just the second Republican senator from the state to win since 1966 and the first since Scott Brown in 2010. Tuesday’s debate was headlined by Markey’s repeated attempts to cast Deaton as another GOP soldier for President Donald Trump’s agenda. The senator emphasized the importance of a Democratic majority in the Senate to place checks on the president. Deaton subsequently distanced himself from the MAGA base and painted himself as a bipartisan politician throughout the debate. His attacks centered on the progressive senator’s “extreme” positions and shortcomings in delivering promises across 50 years in Congress.

Here are 5 takeaways from Tuesday’s debate:A focus on Donald Trump The candidates’ respective relationships to President Donald Trump proved to be the largest point of tension between the two.Advertisement:Markey, who voted against 21 of Trump’s 22 cabinet appointees in 2025, positioned himself as a staunch opponent to the president during the debate. He strove to paint Deaton as nothing more than a cog to further Trump’s agenda.Markey invoked the president’s name more than 40 times throughout the hour-long debate, including in the first sentence of his opening remarks.“I’m going to Washington to be a check on Donald Trump. Mr. Deaton is going to Washington to be a blank check for Donald Trump,” Markey said in his opening statement. In a state where UNH polling shows nearly three-quarters of residents disapprove of the president, Markey’s messaging aligns with residents ahead of the midterm.Deaton tried to paint the senator as giving broken-record responses that failed to address the Republican as a candidate.“You notice how many times he talks about Trump, Trump, Trump,” Deaton said during the debate. He later added, “Senator, my God, … I’m John Deaton, and I’m the one that is debating you, not Donald Trump.”Deaton has made his self-described distance from Trump and the Republican MAGA base a key point in his campaign. During the debate, Deaton said he has never endorsed or voted for the president. Deaton differs from the MAGA base on several key policies, as a pro-abortion rights, anti-Iran war candidate. A split on partisanshipDeaton has positioned himself as more of a bipartisan, independent candidate who would work with both sides of the aisle. But, he said, his opponent is a “partisan person,”  who will not oppose anyone wearing a “Democrat jersey.” Advertisement:“I wear an American jersey. I call President Trump out. I’ll call a Democrat president out. We’ve got to stop hating each other and dividing each other,” Deaton said.Republican Senate nominee John Deaton during Tuesday’s debate in Boston. – WBZ-TVAt one point in the debate, Deaton said he wished Markey was more open to working with the other side — he pointed to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s relationship with the president.“Mamdani calls Trump a fascist. He calls him a misogynist, a racist. But then he goes to Washington and works for New York City,” Deaton said. “Go to Washington and work for the people of Massachusetts, regardless if it’s Trump, regardless if it’s … AOC. I’ll do that.”Markey said Deaton wants voters to believe in a “fantasy land,” where Republicans who buck the president’s agenda don’t face consequences from the MAGA base. He specifically pointed to Republican senators who opposed the president and either didn’t file for reelection or lost the following election, such as Thom Tillis and Bill Cassidy.“Right out of Godfather Part One, [Trump] gives them each an offer they can’t refuse. If they don’t do what he wants, they’re out,” Markey said.Advertisement:Markey characterized Deaton’s attempt to be both independent and a Republican as an “oxymoron.”“The ‘R’ on your jersey, Mr. Deaton, will just stand for ‘rubber stamp’ if you go down there,” Markey said. “You will be in the majority, and Donald Trump and those Republicans will once again control every single committee.”Career politicians and red herringsIn Deaton’s opening statement, he stressed that he isn’t running against the 80-year-old senator because of Markey’s age. However, he attacked various “regrets” throughout Markey’s 50-year career in Congress.For example, he pointed to Markey’s support for a ban on abortion in the 1970s — a position Markey changed in 1983, according to The Boston Globe. He also pointed to Markey’s vote to authorize the Iraq war — a position the senator says he now regrets, according to WBUR.“Senator Markey is just same old, same old, 53 years of trying to get it done. Never gets it done, even when his party’s in control,” Deaton said. Markey brushed off the attacks as “red herrings” meant to take away from the issues at the center of the election, such as rising prices for gas, food, electricity, and healthcare.“It’s all about Trump’s policies, which have had a severe adverse impact on ordinary families watching this debate tonight,” Markey said. “If all it is is a continuation of business as usual … then they’re going to continue to suffer the way they are right now.”Healthcare, energy, and AIWhen it came to policy debate between the two candidates, there was a surprising amount of overlap in their positions. However, the two often differed in the means to get to those ends. US Senator Ed Markey during Tuesday’s debate in Boston. – WBZ-TVMarkey, a firm progressive, continued to push for Medicare for all throughout the debate. He cited a 2025 report by the Boston Public Health Commission which found a 23-year gap in life expectancy between Roxbury and Back Bay residents.Advertisement:While Deaton said he supports more affordable health care, he called Markey’s position “extreme.” Deaton said he instead  has a plan to break up the few “vertically integrated insurance companies” that control a majority of Americans’ healthcare. Both candidates supported various kinds of clean energy solutions. Markey said the Green New Deal, which he co-sponsored, led to 93 percent of electric generating capacity in the country coming from wind, solar, and battery storage — a finding reported by the U.S. Energy Information Administration in 2026.Deaton said he supported a “multifaceted” approach to energy with a belief in solar and geothermal energy. He also emphasized his support for nuclear energy.Both Markey and Deaton also supported safeguards around artificial intelligence.Markey, who has introduced nearly a dozen bills to create safeguards around AI, was vehement about placing guardrails on the technology during the debate. He said AI regulations are currently handled by Silicon Valley billionaires and agreements between Trump and AI CEOs.If reelected, Markey said a Democratic majority would call AI “bros” to testify in front of Congress and be held accountable.Deaton acknowledged the potential advantages of AI, saying the technology could help end cancer or hunger, but he said he worries about elderly residents who can be “taken advantage of” by AI.A second debate?While Tuesday evening was the only scheduled debate between the two candidates, Deaton asked Markey for a second debate in western Massachusetts at the end of Tuesday’s debate.Advertisement:“You’re a very good debater,” Deaton said. “Can we agree right now, Senator?”Deaton held his hand out towards Markey, but the senator didn’t accept the invitation. “We have seen the clear differences between us,” Markey said. “The people of Massachusetts right now have had more than enough information given to them so they can make a decision on election day.”

Incumbent Democratic Sen. Ed Markey and Republican challenger John Deaton faced off in the final debate before Massachusetts voters head to the polls.

At the debate hosted by WBZ-TV, the two rivals went back and forth on a number of issues, including on health care and affordability.


"We do have a medical system in crisis," Markey said. "We have to have a system that finally, once and for all, reaches everyone in our nation."

"If you give me one thing to work on when I go to Washington, it will be health care," Deaton said.

Still, the Republican was critical of Markey's health care priorities.

"Medicare for all -- two thirds of the Senate Democrats don't support it," Deaton said. "I've got a real plan that breaks up the three vertically-integrated insurance companies."

								Democratic Sen. Ed Markey fended off a primary challenge from Rep. Seth Moulton and will face Republican John Deaton in November.
							
The candidates also sparred on energy costs.

Deaton said high utility bills in Massachusetts are "because of these alternative energy mandates."

Markey said that if Deaton is elected, he'll "make it impossible for us to break our dependence upon oil and gas."

Markey and Deaton agreed on a need to establish more guardrails for artificial intelligence.

"Unless we interject some accountability, Donald Trump is just going to have a moral agreement handshake with them," Markey said. "We need a Democratic Senate so we start to have the hearings on this issue."

"We need safeguards," Deaton said. "I'm scared about our seniors, I really am, because our seniors can actually be taken advantage of."

After the debate, both candidates continued to make their pitches to voters.

"If experience could fix Massachusetts, it wouldn't be so broken right now," Deaton said. "I'm here offering an alternative to the status quo."

Opinion | Why John Deaton thinks you should vote for a Republican

And if Democrats win the Senate? Well, the Republican president will still be in power for the next two years, and it could help the state to have an interlocutor with the White House.Get College TownA weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.Enter EmailIt’s an idea that Deaton, 59, is pitching in an attempt to turn what might be his biggest liability into an asset in his uphill battle against 80-year-old Markey. Not surprisingly in deep blue Massachusetts, Markey has made Deaton’s party ID the centerpiece of the campaign against him. “Mr. Deaton is the elephant in the room. He’s going to be another vote for Donald Trump down on the floor in the United States Senate,” Markey said during the debate. “He will be the key vote giving the majority to the Republicans to keep their monopoly in the House, Senate, and presidency.”Never mind that Deaton says he has never voted for Trump and proffers a strong antiestablishment sentiment; he carries the scarlet “R” next to his name. But it’s being the elephant in the room that Deaton, a former Marine and attorney who once challenged Senator Elizabeth Warren, sees as the reason he needs to be in this Senate seat. “Ed Markey thinks [me being the key vote] is the reason to not vote for me, but that’s the most important and best reason to vote for me,” he told me. “It would really give Massachusetts a voice. In a divided Senate, the votes are so close.”The Senate is currently balanced 53 to 47 for Republicans, but polls suggest Republicans may lose some ground in the midterms. Republicans would still control the chamber in the result of a 50-50 tie. There is some precedent for the role Deaton wants to play — Senator Susan Collins makes much the same case as a Republican in Maine, arguing that she’s been able to deliver for the state by occupying the Senate’s center. Deaton acknowledges what he’s up against in a state that hasn’t sent a Republican to Congress since Scott Brown won Ted Kennedy’s seat in 2010. “I’m not delusional,” he told me. “I am very curious.” Curious, that is, about how many people who are tired of one-party rule will turn out to vote for him over Markey, and whether his pragmatic case that Massachusetts will benefit from having representation from both parties will gain traction. In many ways, Deaton does fit into the Brown and Charlie Baker mold that moderate Republicanism has found successful in Massachusetts. He’s prochoice and supports gay marriage, yet he also wants to deregulate the energy and housing markets and supports border security.A Detroit-area native, he fits well into the Massachusetts ethos as a veteran and cancer survivor who’s a bit rough around the edges but is compassionate toward the most vulnerable. During the debate, he seemed teary during his opener talking about hungry children, as he recalls being one.He points to Republican and Democrat senators who don’t always vote along party lines, such as Rand Paul, Thom Tillis, or John Fetterman. Plus, he argues, he’ll work with the next president on Massachusetts’ terms, while he says Markey will simply refuse to work with Republicans.If Deaton wins, he says his first priority would be to fight to lower health care costs. Republicans haven’t offered a legitimate alternative to the Affordable Care Act, he argues. He also wants to break up the big three pharmacy benefit managers that act as middlemen between drug companies, insurers, and pharmacies (the three PBMs are owned by CVS Health, The Cigna Group, and UnitedHealth Group). He would also fight to decrease energy costs by bringing back nuclear power to Massachusetts. He pointed out that when Markey, a longtime foe of nuclear energy, was chair of the Environment and Public Works subcommittee, he was one of two votes in 2024 against the bill that cleared the way for nuclear supply nationwide.Deaton may be right that Markey’s political careerism and 53 years in office is making him increasingly complacent. Spouting about the Green New Deal and “Medicare for all” or refusing to work with the current administration might win him votes but amounts to political posturing, not creating tangible change.Deaton’s bet is that if Massachusetts truly prides itself on progress, then voters should consider a candidate who might actually get things done in a divided Washington.Kara Bettis Carvalho can be reached at kara.carvalho@globe.com. Keller: Deaton brought fire against Markey in Massachusetts Senate debate, but math not in his favor


                                                                                                                                        
                                                                

  
      
    
        



  
    
                                      
                          
            
    
      

      
      
      

                
    By
                        
              
                            
          
              
                                  
                  
                
                
                  Jon  Keller

                                  
              

                              
                  Jon Keller is the political analyst for WBZ-TV News. His "Keller @ Large" reports on a wide range of topics are regularly featured during WBZ News at 5 and 6 p.m.
                
              
              Read Full Bio
            

          

                      
  

          
            Updated on:  October 14, 2026 / 11:51 AM EDT
            / CBS Boston
          
        

          
        
          
          Add CBS News on Google
        
      
        
  


  
  
    The opinions expressed below are Jon Keller's, not those of WBZ-TV, CBS News or Skydance.Republican Massachusetts Senate nominee John Deaton is not stupid. He knows he's a massive underdog in his race against incumbent Ed Markey, trailing by a RealClearPolitics polling average of 23 points, a yawning gap that has never shown any sign of closing.And he can read the national polls too. "We all know that the Democrats are going to win the House, and the Democrats are going to win the Senate," Deaton said in Tuesday night's WBZ debate. "You have a chance to send a nonpartisan person like me [to Washington] who will really put America first and decide, 'Is it good for Massachusetts and America?' And if it is, I'll support it."This is the choice cut from Deaton's beef with Markey - his argument, aimed at independents and disgruntled Democrats, that Markey is too partisan to be trusted. After agreeing with Markey that Donald Trump's war with Iran is illegal and foolish, Deaton cited military ventures under Democratic presidents that "you never said a word [about] because they wear Democrat jerseys. I wear an American jersey. I call President Trump out, I'll call a Democrat president out."
    
    
                                    
      

      
          
        
        
                  Republican Massachusetts Senate candidate John Deaton and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey during the WBZ debate. 
        
                  
            
                CBS Boston

                          
              
      
    
  Unfortunately for Deaton, the math is not in his favor. Mr. Trump's job approval in Massachusetts is at a record low in the most recent polling last month, third worst in the nation. Just 7% of Democrats approve, along with a pitiful 12% of independents. Even among Republicans, approval of Mr. Trump has tumbled to 64%, down from 79% in August.And by emphasizing his distaste for much of the Trump agenda and his refusal to vote for Mr. Trump, Deaton has even shrunk the available pool of Republican votes, not that they amount to much.So, it was no wonder that Markey made a run at the world record for disparaging references to Mr. Trump in an hourlong debate set by Gov. Maura Healey just last week. Trump has "declared war on the Massachusetts economy" and "targeted" Markey's neighbors in Malden, he said. And right off the top he cast Deaton as "the elephant in the room," a poseur who "gave $350,000 to the Republican Party in order to buy this nomination. He's got an R on his jersey, he bought that R … He's trying to pretend that he's an independent and that he's a Republican at the same time. That's an oxymoron. It's like trying to be a carnivorous vegetarian, you just can't get away with that."

    
    
Ouch.Deaton was well-prepared, brought the fire, and landed a number of blows that at times appeared to make Markey wince. But the incumbent never took the bait, pivoting away from every taunt with a Trump-related counter.In this state, this year, with this president insisting voters pretend he's on the ballot, that should be more than enough.

Nearly half of voters in pre-election poll say Mass. has gotten worse over 4 years


                                    Many respondents to a new poll believe Massachusetts has become a worse place to live over the past four years and they still favor keeping incumbent Gov. Maura Healey in the corner office over her Republican opponent.More than 42% of respondents to a new Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll released on Tuesday said they thought Massachusetts has become “a little” or “significantly” worse over the past four years and 40% said the state has stayed the same. More than 52% of respondents said they felt like Massachusetts was heading in the right direction.More than 58% of respondents said they’d favor reelecting Healey over tapping her GOP opponent Mike Minogue, who earned 36% of respondents’ backing. Healey led Minogue 56-31 in a UMass Amherst / WCVB poll released on Monday.
More than 34% of respondents in the Suffolk/Globe poll said Healey has performed better than expected throughout her first term. About 35% said she has done worse than expected.When it comes to who respondents view as responsible for the state of Massachusetts’ economy, Healey (34%) and President Donald Trump (more than 33%) are almost tied. Almost 35% of respondents said the state’s economy is “fair” and more than 38% called it “good” or “excellent.” More than 23% said the Bay State economy is “poor.”Throughout this election cycle, Healey has continuously bashed Trump and tried to connect him to Minogue, who has donated to Trump and other Republicans. Minogue has tried to distance himself from the president by avoiding using his name and appealing to voters in the center of the political spectrum.About 60% of respondents said they would not, or be less likely to, vote for a Republican candidate who has voted for or supported Trump. Almost 31% said it makes no difference to them.About 21% of respondents said that they had never heard of Minogue, a first-time candidate and former CEO of Abiomed, and 1.6% said they didn’t know Healey. More than 56% of respondents who know of Healey have a favorable opinion of her. More than 28% of respondents said they had a favorable view of Minogue.The poll surveyed 500 registered voters from Oct. 14 through Oct. 17 and has a 4.4% margin of error.
In a rare moment of agreement, Healey and Minogue have both called for a suspension of the state’s gas tax as prices at the pump have risen. Eleven percent of respondents said gas prices were their greatest source of financial stress.Also, while temperatures are dropping and energy prices are rising, utility/heating bills were the most common financial strain respondents listed with almost 23% saying it was their greatest fiscal burden.Other poll resultsThe poll found respondents favored all of the state’s constitutional officers seeking reelection.More than 54% said they’d vote to reelect Democratic Attorney General Andrea Campbell over her Republican challenger Michael Walsh, who earned around 28% of respondents support.Secretary of State Bill Galvin, a Democrat seeking a record ninth term, received almost 67% of respondents’ support over his Republican contender Anne Brensley, who earned more than 21% of respondents’ backing. Brensley originally ran for lieutenant governor but was knocked off that ballot as a result of allegedly fraudulent signatures and switched to running to become the state’s elections chief.Democratic Treasurer Deb Goldberg beat her Republican opponent Elizabeth Dionne in the poll (58% to more than 24%) as she is seeking a fourth term.Democratic Auditor Diana DiZoglio led her Libertarian opponent Al Ozonoff (more than 64% to 15%) in the poll. DiZoglio is the only constitutional office holder not facing a Republican opponent.U.S. Sen Ed Markey, who was first sent to Washington D.C. as a congressman in 1976, held a comfortable lead of 60% over Republican John Deaton’s almost 31%. Like Minogue, Almost 45% of respondents said they had never heard of Deaton and 75% of those who had held an unfavorable opinion of him.Ballot questionsAround 21% of respondents said they plan to vote “yes” on Question 8 to essentially repeal the state’s recreational marijuana laws and about 71% said they were against abolishing the decade-old industry that was established through a ballot question. Also, more than 60% of respondents said they had never purchased cannabis from a dispensary.On the other repeal question going before voters, more than 57% of respondents also said they’d like to keep the state’s 2024 gun law, saying they would vote yes on Question 9.Question 1, which subjects the governor’s office and Legislature to the state’s public records law, was also popular with more than 62% of respondents saying they would vote for it. Question 4 that proposes allowing Election Day registration also earned more than 59% of respondents’ support. Another question earning support from respondents was Question 2, which allows public defenders to unionize with about 56% saying they’d vote “yes.”The margins were close on other questions: Question 5 changing the cap on state revenue collections and making taxpayer rebates likelier (40% yes and almost 38% no); Question 7 allowing single-family homes to be built on smaller lots (about 41% yes and 40% no); Question 3 to create an all-party primary election system (about 47% yes and 41% no); and Question 6 proposing to create a fund for natural resource conservation from taxes collected on sporting goods (almost 49% yes and 39% no).

Your options for votingOnce you’ve registered and done your research on the issues and candidates, it’s time to vote.Absentee voting and vote by mailIf you won’t be home on Election Day, are serving in the military or living overseas, are currently incarcerated, or you have religious beliefs or a disability that prevent you from voting in person at your polling place, you may be eligible to vote with an absentee ballot. You can apply by mail, email or fax through your local election office. You’d be using the same ballots as voters who vote by mail and need to meet the same deadlines.Click here to get more information about options for individuals who are currently or formerly incarcerated.All other voters are entitled to vote by mail for any reason, as long as you’re already registered to vote. Every Massachusetts resident should be sent an application in the mail before the election. An official ballot drop box for the city of Melrose.

Your proof of identification can be a license, recent utility bill or a copy of your rental lease.If you don’t have your ID with you, it’s your right to request a provisional ballot.
